query_text: how do bacteriophages differ from antibiotics

content.text:
Bacteriophages (“phages”) and antibiotics both can fight bacterial infections, but they work very differently.

| Feature | Bacteriophages | Antibiotics |
|---|---|---|
| **What they are** | Viruses that infect bacteria | Chemical drugs, natural or synthetic |
| **Target** | Usually very specific bacterial strains or species | Often broader groups of bacteria |
| **How they work** | Attach to bacteria, inject genetic material, replicate, and often burst the bacterial cell | Interfere with bacterial processes like cell-wall synthesis, protein production, DNA replication, or metabolism |
| **Specificity** | Highly specific; may spare normal microbiome | Can kill harmful and beneficial bacteria |
| **Resistance** | Bacteria can become resistant to phages, but phages can also evolve in response | Bacteria can develop antibiotic resistance, which can spread widely |
| **Use in medicine** | Used in some places and studied increasingly, especially for resistant infections | Widely used and standardized globally |
| **Dosing behavior** | Can multiply at the infection site if matching bacteria are present | Drug levels generally decrease over time and require repeated dosing |
| **Limitations** | Need to match the right phage to the bacterial strain; immune system may neutralize them; regulation and standardization are more complex | Can cause side effects, disrupt microbiome, and drive antibiotic resistance |

In short: **antibiotics are chemical agents that broadly inhibit or kill bacteria**, while **bacteriophages are bacteria-infecting viruses that usually target specific bacteria very precisely**. Phages may be especially useful against antibiotic-resistant bacteria, but they typically require more individualized matching than antibiotics.
